blocks.prompt: The Gardener Who Never Meant To
blocks.text: Watch a squirrel in the fall and you will see it working. It picks up a nut, turns it over in its paws, and runs off with it. It digs a small hole, drops the nut in, pushes the dirt back, and pats it down. Then it does it again. And again. Before winter arrives, a gray squirrel may bury a few thousand nuts, one at a time, all over the yard. How does it ever find them? For a long time, people thought squirrels just sniffed around and got lucky. Then scientists tested it. A squirrel remembers where its own nuts are. It steers by landmarks, like a stump or a rock or a fence post, the same way you know which house on the street is yours. Its nose helps too, especially under snow. Even so, the squirrel never digs up all of them. The nuts it misses sit in the ground all winter. In the spring, some of them sprout. That is how a squirrel plants trees without meaning to. Many of the oaks in a park were put there by an animal that forgot.

blocks.prompt: The Squirrel's Secret System
blocks.text: A squirrel in the fall looks like it is in a hurry, and it is. Tree squirrels do not hibernate. They stay awake through the whole winter, when there is almost nothing left to eat, so everything they will need has to be hidden before the cold arrives. Here is the odd part. A squirrel does not build one big pantry. It buries its nuts one at a time, in hundreds and hundreds of separate holes, spread all over its territory. Scientists call this scatter hoarding. It sounds careless. It is actually clever. If a squirrel kept everything in one pile, a single thief could clear it out in an afternoon. Scattered nuts have to be stolen one by one. But scattering only works if the squirrel can find its way back, and it can. Squirrels remember their hiding places by using landmarks, a stump, a rock, a fence post, and they seem to sort their nuts by type, keeping the hickory nuts in one area and the acorns in another. That way, hunting for a hickory nut means searching part of the yard instead of all of it. Their noses fill in the gaps, and a squirrel can smell a nut buried under snow. Squirrels also lie. If one notices another squirrel watching, it may dig a hole, drop nothing into it, push the dirt back, and pat it flat, then hurry off with the nut still in its mouth. The watcher digs up an empty hole. The nut is somewhere else entirely. And a squirrel that hides food still has to open it. Its front teeth never stop growing, so gnawing has to wear them down as fast as they grow. That is why a squirrel always seems to be chewing on something.

blocks.prompt: A Memory Made of Maps
blocks.text: In September, a gray squirrel starts working like it has a deadline, because it does. It will not hibernate. Tree squirrels stay awake all winter, and a winter forest offers almost nothing to eat. Everything the animal needs between November and March has to go into the ground before the ground freezes. So it buries. One nut at a time, in a shallow hole, spread across a territory that can cover several acres. Biologists call this scatter hoarding, and it is a strange choice. Plenty of animals do the opposite. A red squirrel builds a single pantry, piling cones into one great heap and defending the heap all winter. A gray squirrel spreads its entire future across thousands of holes and guards none of them. The logic is insurance. A guarded pantry is one bad afternoon away from ruin, because a thief that finds it finds everything. Thousands of scattered nuts cannot be taken all at once. Each one has to be found separately, and finding is expensive. The cost of that strategy is memory. A squirrel that cannot relocate its own caches has simply thrown its winter away. For years, people assumed squirrels wandered until they smelled something and got lucky. Then researchers tested it directly. The squirrels recovered their own caches far more often than chance would allow, and more often than they found caches other squirrels had buried. They were not sniffing at random. They were remembering. They navigate by landmarks, a stump, a fence post, the angle between two trees, the same way you find your own front door without reading the number on it. There is evidence they organize as well as remember. Watch closely and a squirrel appears to sort by kind, filing hickory nuts in one region of its territory and acorns in another. Researchers call this spatial chunking. It is what you are doing when you keep socks in one drawer and shirts in another, and it means a squirrel hunting for a hickory nut searches one part of its map instead of the whole thing. Smell fills in the rest. A squirrel can locate a nut under a foot of snow by scent alone, which is why a damp, cold day is a good digging day and a frozen one is not. None of it works perfectly. The squirrel misses some. Those become trees.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Oaks pay squirrels in fat and starch to move their seeds
Red oak acorns are high in bitter tannins
White oak acorns sprout in fall; red oak acorns wait for spring
Squirrels bite the embryo out of white oak acorns before caching
Deceptive caching: a faked burial for a watching thief
Squirrels navigate back by landmarks and sort stores by type

blocks.prompt: The Squirrel and the Oak: An Argument in Slow Motion
blocks.text: Every fall, a gray squirrel does a job it never agreed to. It gathers acorns, carries them away from the tree that made them, and buries them one by one across a territory that may run to several acres. It repeats this thousands of times. It believes it is feeding itself for winter. It is also, with no intention whatsoever, planting the forest. Consider the oak's problem. An oak cannot walk. If its acorns dropped and sprouted directly beneath it, its own offspring would spend their lives in its shade, crowded and starved of light, competing with their parent for the same water. The oak needs its seeds carried away, and it has no way to carry them. So it makes an offer. It packs each acorn with fat and starch, more than enough to be worth an animal's trouble, and releases thousands at once. Some get eaten immediately. Some get hauled off and buried, and the ones the squirrel never returns for are, from the tree's perspective, delivered. This is not a friendship. It is closer to a long argument, and both sides have spent millions of years sharpening their positions. Look at what an oak puts into an acorn besides food. Red oak acorns are loaded with tannins, bitter compounds that make them slow to eat and hard to digest. White oak acorns carry far less. You would expect a squirrel to prefer the sweeter white oak acorn, and it does. It eats those on the spot. The bitter red oak acorns it buries. That looks backward until you check the acorns' schedules. White oak acorns germinate almost immediately in fall. Bury one and by spring it is a seedling, which is no longer a meal. Red oak acorns wait until spring to sprout, so they keep in the ground all winter. The squirrel is not sorting by taste. It is sorting by shelf life. It eats what will spoil and banks what will keep. Then the squirrels pushed back. Researchers have watched gray squirrels take a white oak acorn, bite the embryo out of its tip, and bury what remains. An acorn without its embryo cannot sprout, so the squirrel has converted a perishable seed into a storable one. The tree loses that acorn completely. Its bribe has been accepted and its offspring discarded. There is also the matter of theft. A buried nut only pays off if the squirrel who buried it is the one who digs it up, and squirrels rob one another constantly. So a squirrel that senses it is being watched will sometimes perform the entire routine, dig, push, pat the soil flat, and stroll away with the nut still in its mouth. Biologists call this deceptive caching. The animal has staged a hiding place for an audience. To make any of this pay, the squirrel has to remember, and it largely does. It navigates back by landmarks rather than by scent alone, and it appears to file its stores by kind, hickories in one region, acorns in another, which shrinks each search. Its nose covers the gaps, even under snow. But no memory is perfect, and here is the point: it does not need to be. The nuts left in the ground are not the squirrel's failure. They are the oak's payment, and the only part of the bargain the tree ever actually wanted. So when you see a squirrel patting down a patch of dirt, understand what you are watching. Not a hoarder. A negotiation, conducted by an animal convinced it is winning.
